To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fermentation of glucose by the feces of a breast-fed human infant changes with age.
the fermentation of glucose changes after the neonate is colonized with microbes.

the fermentative pathways for glucose fermentation change from the Embden- Meyerhof-Parnas to the Bifido- bacterium pathway with age and the fermentations of glucose by the colonic microbiota of breast-fed infants are similar to fermentations by Escherichia and Streptococcus spp.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the human colonic microbial fermentation and the metabolic pathways used by these microbes.
the evolution of the microbial fermentation in the neonatal gut.
the evolution of the colonic microbial fermentation from the time of microbial colonization to 158 d.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fermentation of glucose changes from that of E. coli and streptroccocci to the Bifido pathway with the increase in acetate formation after 117 d.

the fermentation of glucose in the human colon is dominated by the Bifidbacterium pathway in the neonate, and that it changes to the Embden-Meyershof-Parnas and Entner-Doudoroff pathways after the neonate becomes an infant.
the fecal fermentation of glucose changes with the age of the infant and that the change is related to the development of the colonic microbiota.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, during the first 3 to 4 mo of life, the colonic fermentation in the breast-fed infant is dominated by the Bifidoflora and the fermentation is similar to that of the Bifodobacterium fermentation.
the fecal flora from breast-fed infants < 1 mo old ferment glucose to ethanol, acetate, lactate, succinate, formate and CO2 and H2.

the colonic microflora of the breast-fed infant is similar to that of adults, with the exception that the Embden-Mayerhof-Parnas fermentation pathway is used by the fecal microflora of infants up to 4 mo of age.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fermentation of glucose in the colon of a breast-fed human infant changes with age, with a shift from an E. coli-like to a Bifidobacterial-like fermentation.
the fermentation of carbohydrates by the fecal microbes of a breast-fed human infant undergoes significant changes during the first few months of life.
the fermentation pattern of the fecal flora in the infant colon evolves from a pattern that is similar to that of E. coli to a pattern similar to that of Bifidobacteria.
